iterations.explanation: The taxonomy is organized along the machine learning workflow, beginning with data ingestion, storage, validation, and dataset construction; continuing through feature representation, training, evaluation, packaging, and reproducibility; and ending with deployment, serving, scaling, monitoring, governance, retraining, and retirement. Each dimension names one architectural decision, while its values represent commonly adopted alternatives, explicitly rejected practices, or outcomes that result from the decision. Relations connect upstream data and modeling choices to downstream serving, monitoring, and lifecycle consequences. The design space emphasizes recurring practitioner trade-offs: freshness versus complexity, offline reproducibility versus adaptation speed, predictive quality versus latency and cost, portability versus framework-specific optimization, and rapid deployment versus safety and rollback control. Governance and security are treated as cross-cutting constraints rather than a final workflow step because they influence data access, storage, training, serving, monitoring, and retirement throughout the system lifecycle.

clusters.name: Data Ingestion Strategy
clusters.description: How training, validation, and production data are acquired and brought into the machine learning system. Values answer whether data is collected in batches, streamed, or obtained through a hybrid approach, balancing latency, completeness, cost, and operational complexity.

relations.reading: Data Ingestion Strategy affects Data Storage and Access because ingestion frequency and ordering determine suitable storage and retrieval mechanisms
relations.rationale: Streaming and batch ingestion impose different requirements on retention, partitioning, replay, and query access.

relations.reading: Data Ingestion Strategy affects Data Quality and Validation because ingestion paths determine where and when quality checks can be applied
relations.rationale: Streaming pipelines often require online validation, while batch pipelines can support more comprehensive offline checks.

relations.reading: Data Ingestion Strategy affects Production Serving Strategy because online feature and prediction paths may need compatible real-time data feeds
relations.rationale: Low-latency serving commonly depends on continuously updated inputs and feature values.

values.label: Batch ingestion
values.description: Periodic extraction and loading of data in bounded batches.

values.label: Stream ingestion
values.description: Continuous ingestion of events or records as they arrive.

values.label: Hybrid batch-stream ingestion
values.description: A combined architecture using streams for fresh data and batches for backfills, historical loads, or reconciliation.

values.label: Low-latency data availability
values.description: An operational outcome in which newly arriving data becomes usable quickly, usually at the cost of additional infrastructure and consistency complexity.

clusters.name: Data Storage and Access Strategy
clusters.description: How raw, curated, feature, and training data are retained and made available to processing and serving components. The choice is driven by scale, access patterns, durability, governance, cost, and reproducibility.

relations.reading: Data Storage and Access Strategy affects Feature Representation Strategy because storage layout and retrieval latency constrain how features can be materialized and reused
relations.rationale: Feature stores, warehouses, lakes, and serving databases provide different support for offline computation and online lookup.

relations.reading: Data Storage and Access Strategy constrains Production Serving Strategy because storage latency and availability limit feasible online prediction paths
relations.rationale: Online serving cannot depend on stores that are too slow, unavailable, or expensive for request-time access.

relations.reading: Data Storage and Access Strategy affects Governance and Security Controls because retention and access mechanisms determine how data can be controlled and audited
relations.rationale: Storage choices define encryption, access boundaries, lineage, retention, and deletion capabilities.

values.label: Object-storage data lake
values.description: Durable files or objects in low-cost shared storage, commonly organized by partition and format.

values.label: Analytical warehouse
values.description: Managed structured storage optimized for governed analytical queries and transformations.

values.label: Operational database
values.description: Transactional or key-value storage used when application-integrated access and low-latency lookups are required.

values.label: Feature store
values.description: A specialized system coordinating offline feature computation and online feature retrieval.

values.label: Unmanaged local files
values.description: Ad hoc local or developer-specific storage without shared lineage, access control, or reproducible retrieval.

values.label: Centralized data access
values.description: An outcome in which teams can consistently discover, retrieve, and reuse governed datasets and features.

clusters.name: Data Quality and Validation Strategy
clusters.description: How correctness, completeness, schema compatibility, drift, and anomalous values are detected and handled before data reaches training or production.

relations.reading: Data Quality and Validation Strategy affects Dataset Construction Strategy because validation findings determine which records and time windows are eligible for modeling
relations.rationale: Quality rules can remove, repair, quarantine, or reject data used in datasets.

relations.reading: Data Quality and Validation Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because production checks often reuse training-time assumptions and quality baselines
relations.rationale: Monitoring must detect violations of the data contracts and distributions assumed during model development.

relations.reading: Data Quality and Validation Strategy affects Governance and Security Controls because validation can enforce provenance, privacy, and policy requirements
relations.rationale: Data checks may identify unauthorized fields, sensitive data, missing consent, or invalid lineage.

values.label: Schema and contract validation
values.description: Automated checks for types, columns, ranges, nullability, and producer-consumer contracts.

values.label: Statistical and distribution validation
values.description: Checks for distribution shifts, outliers, missingness changes, and unexpected category or value frequencies.

values.label: Quarantine and remediation workflow
values.description: Isolation of invalid records followed by correction, replacement, or explicit disposition rather than silent ingestion.

values.label: Unvalidated data propagation
values.description: Allowing data to proceed without systematic automated quality checks.

values.label: Higher data reliability
values.description: An outcome in which defective, incompatible, or anomalous inputs are detected before they silently degrade models.

clusters.name: Dataset Construction Strategy
clusters.description: How examples, labels, time windows, and partitions are assembled into datasets for development and evaluation. The choice is driven by leakage risk, representativeness, temporal behavior, class imbalance, and labeling cost.

relations.reading: Dataset Construction Strategy constrains Model Training Strategy because available labels, splits, and sampling determine feasible training procedures
relations.rationale: Training can only use the examples, labels, and partition semantics established during dataset construction.

relations.reading: Dataset Construction Strategy affects Model Evaluation Strategy because evaluation validity depends on how representative and leakage-free the held-out data is
relations.rationale: Random, grouped, temporal, and stratified splits estimate different forms of generalization.

relations.reading: Dataset Construction Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because training populations and label definitions provide baselines for production drift and performance checks
relations.rationale: Monitoring compares live inputs and outcomes against the population and target semantics used to build the model.

values.label: Random stratified partitioning
values.description: Random train, validation, and test partitions preserving important class proportions.

values.label: Time-based partitioning
values.description: Partitions based on chronology to simulate future prediction and avoid using future information.

values.label: Group-aware partitioning
values.description: Partitions that keep related entities, users, devices, or sessions within a single split.

values.label: Resampling and reweighting
values.description: Oversampling, undersampling, or weighting used to address imbalance or differing example importance.

values.label: Random split with leakage
values.description: A superficially convenient split that allows related or future information to cross evaluation boundaries.

values.label: Representative generalization estimate
values.description: An outcome in which offline evaluation more credibly predicts behavior on the intended future or user population.

clusters.name: Feature Representation Strategy
clusters.description: How raw inputs are transformed, selected, stored, and shared as model features. The decision balances predictive signal, serving consistency, latency, interpretability, computation, and maintenance burden.

relations.reading: Feature Representation Strategy affects Model Training Strategy because feature scale, sparsity, dimensionality, and availability determine appropriate algorithms and optimization methods
relations.rationale: Different representations favor different model families and preprocessing pipelines.

relations.reading: Feature Representation Strategy constrains Production Serving Strategy because online predictions require features that can be computed or retrieved within the serving budget
relations.rationale: Features requiring unavailable future data or expensive batch computation cannot be used directly in low-latency serving.

relations.reading: Feature Representation Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because feature distributions and transformation failures are important signals of production degradation
relations.rationale: Monitoring must observe both raw inputs and transformed features when transformations can fail or drift.

values.label: Hand-engineered domain features
values.description: Features designed from domain knowledge, business rules, aggregations, and statistical transformations.

values.label: Learned representations
values.description: Embeddings or other representations learned from data, often by deep models or self-supervised objectives.

values.label: Raw-input modeling
values.description: Models that consume minimally transformed raw inputs and learn much of the representation internally.

values.label: Shared offline-online features
values.description: A feature definition and computation approach designed to keep training and serving feature semantics consistent.

values.label: Training-serving skew
values.description: An outcome in which features are computed differently or from different information during training and production.

clusters.name: Model Training Strategy
clusters.description: How model parameters are learned and updated. Values answer whether training is performed centrally, incrementally, collaboratively, or with transfer and fine-tuning, under constraints of data volume, compute, privacy, and adaptation speed.

relations.reading: Model Training Strategy affects Model Packaging Format because training outputs, preprocessing dependencies, and runtime requirements determine what must be packaged
relations.rationale: Training procedures may produce ensembles, checkpoints, tokenizers, feature transforms, or specialized runtime artifacts.

relations.reading: Model Training Strategy affects Experiment Reproducibility Strategy because distributed, stochastic, and continuously updated training requires corresponding lineage and checkpoint controls
relations.rationale: Reproducing a training result depends on recording data, code, randomness, hardware, and update history.

relations.reading: Model Training Strategy affects Production Serving Strategy because model size, architecture, and update frequency influence serving infrastructure
relations.rationale: Large or frequently updated models require different runtimes, accelerators, rollout mechanisms, and resource budgets.

values.label: Centralized offline training
values.description: Periodic training over centrally accessible historical data, usually producing versioned model artifacts.

values.label: Incremental or online training
values.description: Updating a model continuously or in short intervals as new labeled data arrives.

values.label: Transfer learning and fine-tuning
values.description: Adapting a pretrained model or representation to a target task or domain.

values.label: Federated or distributed privacy-preserving training
values.description: Training across separated data holders while limiting central access to raw data or coordinating computation across workers.

values.label: Untracked manual training
values.description: Ad hoc training performed without repeatable data, code, configuration, or artifact capture.

values.label: Model adaptation speed
values.description: An outcome describing how quickly the model can incorporate new data or changing task conditions.

clusters.name: Model Evaluation Strategy
clusters.description: How candidate models are compared and judged before release. The decision balances predictive metrics, calibration, robustness, fairness, business utility, offline realism, and evaluation cost.

relations.reading: Model Evaluation Strategy affects Deployment Promotion Strategy because release gates and approval criteria depend on what evidence is required
relations.rationale: A deployment pipeline needs explicit thresholds and tests for model quality and risk.

relations.reading: Model Evaluation Strategy affects Production Serving Strategy because latency, resource use, and operational behavior may be part of model acceptance
relations.rationale: A model that is accurate but too slow or expensive cannot satisfy production requirements.

relations.reading: Model Evaluation Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because production monitors should measure the same quality dimensions that justified release
relations.rationale: Offline metrics and risk criteria provide baselines for detecting degradation after deployment.

values.label: Holdout evaluation
values.description: Evaluation on data excluded from model fitting and model-selection decisions.

values.label: Cross-validation
values.description: Repeated training and evaluation across folds to estimate performance and tune models when data is limited.

values.label: Scenario and robustness evaluation
values.description: Testing across subgroups, perturbations, distribution shifts, adversarial cases, or operational edge cases.

values.label: Business and operational evaluation
values.description: Assessment using costs, benefits, calibration, latency, resource use, fairness, or downstream decision outcomes in addition to predictive metrics.

values.label: Single-metric evaluation
values.description: Selecting a model solely by one aggregate predictive metric while ignoring relevant populations, costs, or operational constraints.

values.label: Deployment confidence
values.description: An outcome in which evidence supports a defensible decision about whether a candidate model is suitable for use.

clusters.name: Model Packaging Format
clusters.description: How a trained model and its preprocessing, dependencies, metadata, and runtime are represented for transfer between development and production.

relations.reading: Model Packaging Format constrains Production Serving Strategy because serving runtimes can execute only compatible model and dependency artifacts
relations.rationale: The package format determines supported operators, hardware targets, dependency isolation, and loading behavior.

relations.reading: Model Packaging Format affects Deployment Promotion Strategy because immutable and versioned artifacts make promotion and rollback more reliable
relations.rationale: Deployment systems need identifiable artifacts whose contents do not change after validation.

relations.reading: Model Packaging Format affects Experiment Reproducibility Strategy because captured artifacts preserve the exact model and runtime used for an experiment
relations.rationale: Reproducibility requires more than weights when preprocessing and runtime dependencies affect behavior.

values.label: Framework-native artifact
values.description: A model saved in the format of its training framework together with required preprocessing state.

values.label: Portable interchange artifact
values.description: A framework-independent representation intended to run across compatible serving engines or platforms.

values.label: Containerized model service
values.description: A model, runtime, libraries, and serving code packaged as an isolated deployable container.

values.label: Unversioned model files
values.description: Model files copied or referenced without immutable versioning, dependency capture, or integrity metadata.

values.label: Environment portability
values.description: An outcome in which a validated model behaves consistently across development, testing, and production environments.

clusters.name: Experiment Reproducibility Strategy
clusters.description: How data, code, parameters, environments, random seeds, lineage, and model artifacts are recorded so training results can be repeated or audited.

relations.reading: Experiment Reproducibility Strategy affects Model Training Strategy because recorded lineage and automation determine whether training can be repeated systematically
relations.rationale: Reproducibility practices shape whether training is a controlled pipeline or an ad hoc activity.

relations.reading: Experiment Reproducibility Strategy affects Deployment Promotion Strategy because promotion requires traceability from a production artifact to its validated experiment
relations.rationale: Approvers need to identify what data, code, and configuration produced the candidate.

relations.reading: Experiment Reproducibility Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because monitoring needs model, data, and feature versions to interpret changes
relations.rationale: Without version lineage, a production metric change cannot be reliably attributed or compared.

values.label: Versioned datasets and code
values.description: Explicit versioning of source data, transformations, training code, and configuration.

values.label: Experiment tracking
values.description: Central recording of runs, parameters, metrics, artifacts, and lineage.

values.label: Deterministic pipeline execution
values.description: Controlled environments and seeds that reduce avoidable variation between repeated runs.

values.label: Manual notebook execution
values.description: Training and evaluation performed through undocumented or weakly controlled interactive steps.

values.label: Reproducible model lineage
values.description: An outcome in which a deployed result can be traced back to its inputs, transformations, code, configuration, and evaluation evidence.

clusters.name: Deployment Promotion Strategy
clusters.description: How a validated model is moved into production and how release risk is controlled. The decision is driven by safety, rollback capability, traffic exposure, compliance, and release speed.

relations.reading: Deployment Promotion Strategy affects Infrastructure Scaling Strategy because rollout methods determine how many concurrent versions and traffic paths must be supported
relations.rationale: Canary, shadow, blue-green, and staged releases create different capacity and routing requirements.

relations.reading: Deployment Promotion Strategy affects Production Serving Strategy because rollout requires compatible routing, version selection, and coexistence mechanisms
relations.rationale: Serving infrastructure must support traffic splitting, shadow requests, or rapid version replacement.

relations.reading: Deployment Promotion Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because progressive exposure requires release-specific monitoring and rollback thresholds
relations.rationale: Canaries and staged launches depend on observing behavior before broader exposure.

values.label: Direct replacement
values.description: Replacing the currently serving model with the newly approved model in one release step.

values.label: Blue-green deployment
values.description: Maintaining separate old and new environments and switching traffic between them.

values.label: Canary or staged rollout
values.description: Exposing the new model progressively to a limited or increasing fraction of traffic.

values.label: Shadow deployment
values.description: Running the candidate on production inputs without using its outputs for user-facing decisions.

values.label: Irreversible release
values.description: A release process without a tested rollback or prior-version serving path.

values.label: Controlled release risk
values.description: An outcome in which model changes can be assessed, limited, and reversed without unacceptable service disruption.

clusters.name: Inference Resource and Scaling Strategy
clusters.description: How compute, memory, accelerators, concurrency, and capacity are allocated for prediction workloads. The decision balances latency, throughput, availability, cost, energy use, and model size.

relations.reading: Inference Resource and Scaling Strategy constrains Production Serving Strategy because available capacity and hardware determine feasible serving modes and latency
relations.rationale: Resource choices determine whether a model can be served synchronously, in batches, on specialized hardware, or at a given throughput.

relations.reading: Inference Resource and Scaling Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because saturation, queueing, and resource failures are operational signals
relations.rationale: Monitoring must include infrastructure behavior in addition to prediction quality.

values.label: CPU serving
values.description: Inference on general-purpose CPUs for broad compatibility, moderate cost, and simpler operations.

values.label: Accelerated serving
values.description: Inference using GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, or other specialized hardware for demanding models or throughput.

values.label: Autoscaled serving
values.description: Dynamic allocation of serving capacity in response to traffic or resource demand.

values.label: Batch inference
values.description: Offline or micro-batched prediction for workloads that can trade freshness or per-request latency for efficiency.

values.label: Overprovisioned fixed capacity
values.description: Maintaining permanently large capacity without demand-based adjustment.

values.label: Inference cost and latency trade-off
values.description: An outcome in which lower latency or higher throughput is obtained at increased infrastructure, energy, or operational cost.

clusters.name: Production Serving Strategy
clusters.description: How predictions are exposed to applications and users. Values answer whether inference is synchronous, asynchronous, batch-oriented, embedded, or hybrid, based on latency, reliability, freshness, integration, and cost requirements.

relations.reading: Production Serving Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because serving paths expose different telemetry, delayed labels, and failure modes
relations.rationale: Online APIs, streams, batch jobs, and embedded models require different observability and outcome-linkage mechanisms.

relations.reading: Production Serving Strategy affects Governance and Security Controls because the serving boundary determines authentication, authorization, data exposure, and audit requirements
relations.rationale: An externally reachable prediction API has different security and privacy risks from an internal batch job.

values.label: Synchronous online API
values.description: Returning a prediction within the request-response interaction, usually under a defined latency objective.

values.label: Asynchronous inference service
values.description: Accepting prediction work and returning results later through a queue, callback, or result store.

values.label: Scheduled batch inference
values.description: Producing predictions periodically for a predefined population or dataset.

values.label: Embedded or edge inference
values.description: Executing the model close to the data source or inside an application or device.

values.label: Hybrid serving
values.description: Combining multiple serving modes, such as online predictions with batch fallback or precomputed features.

values.label: Prediction availability and freshness
values.description: An outcome describing how reliably and quickly predictions are produced relative to the consuming application’s needs.

clusters.name: Model Monitoring Strategy
clusters.description: How deployed models and their surrounding systems are observed for service health, data drift, prediction behavior, quality degradation, fairness, and business impact.

relations.reading: Model Monitoring Strategy affects Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy because observed degradation and drift provide triggers for model updates or removal
relations.rationale: Retraining policies commonly depend on monitored thresholds, incidents, and changes in data or outcomes.

relations.reading: Model Monitoring Strategy affects Governance and Security Controls because auditability and responsible operation require evidence about model behavior after release
relations.rationale: Governance often requires monitoring for fairness, policy violations, incidents, and changes in risk.

relations.reading: Model Monitoring Strategy affects Production Serving Strategy because detected failures may require fallback, traffic reduction, or serving changes
relations.rationale: Operational monitoring can trigger failover, rollback, throttling, or disabling of a prediction path.

values.label: Infrastructure and service monitoring
values.description: Monitoring latency, throughput, errors, availability, resource use, queue depth, and saturation.

values.label: Data drift monitoring
values.description: Monitoring changes in input distributions, missingness, schema, feature values, and population composition.

values.label: Prediction and outcome monitoring
values.description: Monitoring prediction distributions, delayed ground-truth performance, calibration, and downstream business outcomes.

values.label: Fairness and subgroup monitoring
values.description: Monitoring quality, error, and impact across relevant demographic, geographic, or operational subgroups.

values.label: Metrics-only monitoring
values.description: Monitoring infrastructure metrics while omitting data, prediction, outcome, or subgroup behavior.

values.label: Production observability
values.description: An outcome in which system and model behavior is visible enough to detect, diagnose, and respond to degradation.

clusters.name: Governance and Security Controls
clusters.description: How privacy, access, accountability, compliance, safety, and responsible-use requirements are enforced across the machine learning lifecycle.

relations.reading: Governance and Security Controls constrain Data Ingestion Strategy because collection and transport must comply with consent, minimization, and access requirements
relations.rationale: Permitted sources, fields, retention, and transport protections limit how data can be acquired.

relations.reading: Governance and Security Controls constrain Data Storage and Access Strategy because storage must enforce retention, isolation, encryption, and authorized access
relations.rationale: Sensitive datasets require appropriate storage controls and auditable access.

relations.reading: Governance and Security Controls constrain Production Serving Strategy because deployed prediction interfaces must enforce identity, authorization, privacy, and abuse controls
relations.rationale: Serving architecture determines exposure to users, applications, and adversarial or unauthorized requests.

relations.reading: Governance and Security Controls affects Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy because compliance obligations can require review, retention, replacement, or removal
relations.rationale: Models and data may need to be retrained, withdrawn, or retired when policies, laws, or risks change.

values.label: Role-based access control
values.description: Restricting data, models, pipelines, and operational actions according to authenticated roles and permissions.

values.label: Privacy-preserving data handling
values.description: Minimization, de-identification, encryption, differential privacy, secure computation, or related protections for sensitive data.

values.label: Lineage and audit trails
values.description: Recording who accessed or changed data, code, models, decisions, and deployments.

values.label: Human review and approval
values.description: Requiring designated people to assess or authorize high-impact data, model, or deployment decisions.

values.label: Unrestricted production access
values.description: Allowing broad access to sensitive data, models, or deployment operations without meaningful controls or auditability.

values.label: Reduced compliance and misuse risk
values.description: An outcome in which unauthorized access, privacy violations, unsafe use, and untraceable changes are less likely.

clusters.name: Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy
clusters.description: How systems decide when to update, rollback, replace, archive, or remove deployed models. The choice is driven by drift, performance, data arrival, incidents, maintenance cost, and changing business or regulatory requirements.

relations.reading: Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy affects Model Training Strategy because update triggers determine whether training is periodic, event-driven, or continuous
relations.rationale: The lifecycle policy determines how often and under what conditions training is initiated.

relations.reading: Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy affects Deployment Promotion Strategy because newly trained or replacement models require a controlled path into and out of production
relations.rationale: Retraining and rollback are only operationally safe when integrated with release and promotion mechanisms.

relations.reading: Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy requires Model Monitoring Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Automated or evidence-based retraining and retirement depend on monitored drift, quality, incidents, and operational signals.

values.label: Scheduled retraining
values.description: Retraining at fixed calendar or data-volume intervals.

values.label: Trigger-based retraining
values.description: Retraining initiated by monitored drift, quality degradation, new labels, incidents, or business events.

values.label: Continuous updating
values.description: Frequent or ongoing model updates as new observations become available.

values.label: Champion-challenger replacement
values.description: Keeping a current champion while evaluating and promoting challenger models against it.

values.label: Model retirement and fallback
values.description: Archiving or disabling a model and reverting to a prior model, rule-based system, or safe default when required.

values.label: Stale model persistence
values.description: Continuing to use a model despite known degradation, changed conditions, or an inability to justify its continued suitability.

values.label: Lifecycle maintenance burden
values.description: An outcome describing the engineering, evaluation, governance, and infrastructure cost of keeping models current and safe.

values.description: An outcome in which features are computed differently or from different information during training and production.

selected_clusters.name: Model Training Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How model parameters are learned and updated. Values answer whether training is performed centrally, incrementally, collaboratively, or with transfer and fine-tuning, under constraints of data volume, compute, privacy, and adaptation speed.

relations.reading: Model Training Strategy affects Model Packaging Format because training outputs, preprocessing dependencies, and runtime requirements determine what must be packaged
relations.rationale: Training procedures may produce ensembles, checkpoints, tokenizers, feature transforms, or specialized runtime artifacts.

relations.reading: Model Training Strategy affects Experiment Reproducibility Strategy because distributed, stochastic, and continuously updated training requires corresponding lineage and checkpoint controls
relations.rationale: Reproducing a training result depends on recording data, code, randomness, hardware, and update history.

relations.reading: Model Training Strategy affects Production Serving Strategy because model size, architecture, and update frequency influence serving infrastructure
relations.rationale: Large or frequently updated models require different runtimes, accelerators, rollout mechanisms, and resource budgets.

values.label: Centralized offline training
values.description: Periodic training over centrally accessible historical data, usually producing versioned model artifacts.

values.label: Incremental or online training
values.description: Updating a model continuously or in short intervals as new labeled data arrives.

values.label: Transfer learning and fine-tuning
values.description: Adapting a pretrained model or representation to a target task or domain.

values.label: Federated or distributed privacy-preserving training
values.description: Training across separated data holders while limiting central access to raw data or coordinating computation across workers.

values.label: Untracked manual training
values.description: Ad hoc training performed without repeatable data, code, configuration, or artifact capture.

values.label: Model adaptation speed
values.description: An outcome describing how quickly the model can incorporate new data or changing task conditions.

selected_clusters.name: Model Evaluation Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How candidate models are compared and judged before release. The decision balances predictive metrics, calibration, robustness, fairness, business utility, offline realism, and evaluation cost.

relations.reading: Model Evaluation Strategy affects Deployment Promotion Strategy because release gates and approval criteria depend on what evidence is required
relations.rationale: A deployment pipeline needs explicit thresholds and tests for model quality and risk.

relations.reading: Model Evaluation Strategy affects Production Serving Strategy because latency, resource use, and operational behavior may be part of model acceptance
relations.rationale: A model that is accurate but too slow or expensive cannot satisfy production requirements.

relations.reading: Model Evaluation Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because production monitors should measure the same quality dimensions that justified release
relations.rationale: Offline metrics and risk criteria provide baselines for detecting degradation after deployment.

values.label: Holdout evaluation
values.description: Evaluation on data excluded from model fitting and model-selection decisions.

values.label: Cross-validation
values.description: Repeated training and evaluation across folds to estimate performance and tune models when data is limited.

values.label: Scenario and robustness evaluation
values.description: Testing across subgroups, perturbations, distribution shifts, adversarial cases, or operational edge cases.

values.label: Business and operational evaluation
values.description: Assessment using costs, benefits, calibration, latency, resource use, fairness, or downstream decision outcomes in addition to predictive metrics.

values.label: Single-metric evaluation
values.description: Selecting a model solely by one aggregate predictive metric while ignoring relevant populations, costs, or operational constraints.

values.label: Deployment confidence
values.description: An outcome in which evidence supports a defensible decision about whether a candidate model is suitable for use.

selected_clusters.name: Model Packaging Format
selected_clusters.description: How a trained model and its preprocessing, dependencies, metadata, and runtime are represented for transfer between development and production.

relations.reading: Model Packaging Format constrains Production Serving Strategy because serving runtimes can execute only compatible model and dependency artifacts
relations.rationale: The package format determines supported operators, hardware targets, dependency isolation, and loading behavior.

relations.reading: Model Packaging Format affects Deployment Promotion Strategy because immutable and versioned artifacts make promotion and rollback more reliable
relations.rationale: Deployment systems need identifiable artifacts whose contents do not change after validation.

relations.reading: Model Packaging Format affects Experiment Reproducibility Strategy because captured artifacts preserve the exact model and runtime used for an experiment
relations.rationale: Reproducibility requires more than weights when preprocessing and runtime dependencies affect behavior.

values.label: Framework-native artifact
values.description: A model saved in the format of its training framework together with required preprocessing state.

values.label: Portable interchange artifact
values.description: A framework-independent representation intended to run across compatible serving engines or platforms.

values.label: Containerized model service
values.description: A model, runtime, libraries, and serving code packaged as an isolated deployable container.

values.label: Unversioned model files
values.description: Model files copied or referenced without immutable versioning, dependency capture, or integrity metadata.

values.label: Environment portability
values.description: An outcome in which a validated model behaves consistently across development, testing, and production environments.

selected_clusters.name: Experiment Reproducibility Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How data, code, parameters, environments, random seeds, lineage, and model artifacts are recorded so training results can be repeated or audited.

relations.reading: Experiment Reproducibility Strategy affects Model Training Strategy because recorded lineage and automation determine whether training can be repeated systematically
relations.rationale: Reproducibility practices shape whether training is a controlled pipeline or an ad hoc activity.

relations.reading: Experiment Reproducibility Strategy affects Deployment Promotion Strategy because promotion requires traceability from a production artifact to its validated experiment
relations.rationale: Approvers need to identify what data, code, and configuration produced the candidate.

relations.reading: Experiment Reproducibility Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because monitoring needs model, data, and feature versions to interpret changes
relations.rationale: Without version lineage, a production metric change cannot be reliably attributed or compared.

values.label: Versioned datasets and code
values.description: Explicit versioning of source data, transformations, training code, and configuration.

values.label: Experiment tracking
values.description: Central recording of runs, parameters, metrics, artifacts, and lineage.

values.label: Deterministic pipeline execution
values.description: Controlled environments and seeds that reduce avoidable variation between repeated runs.

values.label: Manual notebook execution
values.description: Training and evaluation performed through undocumented or weakly controlled interactive steps.

values.label: Reproducible model lineage
values.description: An outcome in which a deployed result can be traced back to its inputs, transformations, code, configuration, and evaluation evidence.

selected_clusters.name: Deployment Promotion Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How a validated model is moved into production and how release risk is controlled. The decision is driven by safety, rollback capability, traffic exposure, compliance, and release speed.

relations.reading: Deployment Promotion Strategy affects Infrastructure Scaling Strategy because rollout methods determine how many concurrent versions and traffic paths must be supported
relations.rationale: Canary, shadow, blue-green, and staged releases create different capacity and routing requirements.

relations.reading: Deployment Promotion Strategy affects Production Serving Strategy because rollout requires compatible routing, version selection, and coexistence mechanisms
relations.rationale: Serving infrastructure must support traffic splitting, shadow requests, or rapid version replacement.

relations.reading: Deployment Promotion Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because progressive exposure requires release-specific monitoring and rollback thresholds
relations.rationale: Canaries and staged launches depend on observing behavior before broader exposure.

values.label: Direct replacement
values.description: Replacing the currently serving model with the newly approved model in one release step.

values.label: Blue-green deployment
values.description: Maintaining separate old and new environments and switching traffic between them.

values.label: Canary or staged rollout
values.description: Exposing the new model progressively to a limited or increasing fraction of traffic.

values.label: Shadow deployment
values.description: Running the candidate on production inputs without using its outputs for user-facing decisions.

values.label: Irreversible release
values.description: A release process without a tested rollback or prior-version serving path.

values.label: Controlled release risk
values.description: An outcome in which model changes can be assessed, limited, and reversed without unacceptable service disruption.

selected_clusters.name: Inference Resource and Scaling Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How compute, memory, accelerators, concurrency, and capacity are allocated for prediction workloads. The decision balances latency, throughput, availability, cost, energy use, and model size.

relations.reading: Inference Resource and Scaling Strategy constrains Production Serving Strategy because available capacity and hardware determine feasible serving modes and latency
relations.rationale: Resource choices determine whether a model can be served synchronously, in batches, on specialized hardware, or at a given throughput.

relations.reading: Inference Resource and Scaling Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because saturation, queueing, and resource failures are operational signals
relations.rationale: Monitoring must include infrastructure behavior in addition to prediction quality.

values.label: CPU serving
values.description: Inference on general-purpose CPUs for broad compatibility, moderate cost, and simpler operations.

values.label: Accelerated serving
values.description: Inference using GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, or other specialized hardware for demanding models or throughput.

values.label: Autoscaled serving
values.description: Dynamic allocation of serving capacity in response to traffic or resource demand.

values.label: Batch inference
values.description: Offline or micro-batched prediction for workloads that can trade freshness or per-request latency for efficiency.

values.label: Overprovisioned fixed capacity
values.description: Maintaining permanently large capacity without demand-based adjustment.

values.label: Inference cost and latency trade-off
values.description: An outcome in which lower latency or higher throughput is obtained at increased infrastructure, energy, or operational cost.

selected_clusters.name: Production Serving Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How predictions are exposed to applications and users. Values answer whether inference is synchronous, asynchronous, batch-oriented, embedded, or hybrid, based on latency, reliability, freshness, integration, and cost requirements.

relations.reading: Production Serving Strategy affects Model Monitoring Strategy because serving paths expose different telemetry, delayed labels, and failure modes
relations.rationale: Online APIs, streams, batch jobs, and embedded models require different observability and outcome-linkage mechanisms.

relations.reading: Production Serving Strategy affects Governance and Security Controls because the serving boundary determines authentication, authorization, data exposure, and audit requirements
relations.rationale: An externally reachable prediction API has different security and privacy risks from an internal batch job.

values.label: Synchronous online API
values.description: Returning a prediction within the request-response interaction, usually under a defined latency objective.

values.label: Asynchronous inference service
values.description: Accepting prediction work and returning results later through a queue, callback, or result store.

values.label: Scheduled batch inference
values.description: Producing predictions periodically for a predefined population or dataset.

values.label: Embedded or edge inference
values.description: Executing the model close to the data source or inside an application or device.

values.label: Hybrid serving
values.description: Combining multiple serving modes, such as online predictions with batch fallback or precomputed features.

values.label: Prediction availability and freshness
values.description: An outcome describing how reliably and quickly predictions are produced relative to the consuming application’s needs.

selected_clusters.name: Model Monitoring Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How deployed models and their surrounding systems are observed for service health, data drift, prediction behavior, quality degradation, fairness, and business impact.

relations.reading: Model Monitoring Strategy affects Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy because observed degradation and drift provide triggers for model updates or removal
relations.rationale: Retraining policies commonly depend on monitored thresholds, incidents, and changes in data or outcomes.

relations.reading: Model Monitoring Strategy affects Governance and Security Controls because auditability and responsible operation require evidence about model behavior after release
relations.rationale: Governance often requires monitoring for fairness, policy violations, incidents, and changes in risk.

relations.reading: Model Monitoring Strategy affects Production Serving Strategy because detected failures may require fallback, traffic reduction, or serving changes
relations.rationale: Operational monitoring can trigger failover, rollback, throttling, or disabling of a prediction path.

values.label: Infrastructure and service monitoring
values.description: Monitoring latency, throughput, errors, availability, resource use, queue depth, and saturation.

values.label: Data drift monitoring
values.description: Monitoring changes in input distributions, missingness, schema, feature values, and population composition.

values.label: Prediction and outcome monitoring
values.description: Monitoring prediction distributions, delayed ground-truth performance, calibration, and downstream business outcomes.

values.label: Fairness and subgroup monitoring
values.description: Monitoring quality, error, and impact across relevant demographic, geographic, or operational subgroups.

values.label: Metrics-only monitoring
values.description: Monitoring infrastructure metrics while omitting data, prediction, outcome, or subgroup behavior.

values.label: Production observability
values.description: An outcome in which system and model behavior is visible enough to detect, diagnose, and respond to degradation.

selected_clusters.name: Governance and Security Controls
selected_clusters.description: How privacy, access, accountability, compliance, safety, and responsible-use requirements are enforced across the machine learning lifecycle.

relations.reading: Governance and Security Controls constrain Data Ingestion Strategy because collection and transport must comply with consent, minimization, and access requirements
relations.rationale: Permitted sources, fields, retention, and transport protections limit how data can be acquired.

relations.reading: Governance and Security Controls constrain Data Storage and Access Strategy because storage must enforce retention, isolation, encryption, and authorized access
relations.rationale: Sensitive datasets require appropriate storage controls and auditable access.

relations.reading: Governance and Security Controls constrain Production Serving Strategy because deployed prediction interfaces must enforce identity, authorization, privacy, and abuse controls
relations.rationale: Serving architecture determines exposure to users, applications, and adversarial or unauthorized requests.

relations.reading: Governance and Security Controls affects Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy because compliance obligations can require review, retention, replacement, or removal
relations.rationale: Models and data may need to be retrained, withdrawn, or retired when policies, laws, or risks change.

values.label: Role-based access control
values.description: Restricting data, models, pipelines, and operational actions according to authenticated roles and permissions.

values.label: Privacy-preserving data handling
values.description: Minimization, de-identification, encryption, differential privacy, secure computation, or related protections for sensitive data.

values.label: Lineage and audit trails
values.description: Recording who accessed or changed data, code, models, decisions, and deployments.

values.label: Human review and approval
values.description: Requiring designated people to assess or authorize high-impact data, model, or deployment decisions.

values.label: Unrestricted production access
values.description: Allowing broad access to sensitive data, models, or deployment operations without meaningful controls or auditability.

values.label: Reduced compliance and misuse risk
values.description: An outcome in which unauthorized access, privacy violations, unsafe use, and untraceable changes are less likely.

selected_clusters.name: Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How systems decide when to update, rollback, replace, archive, or remove deployed models. The choice is driven by drift, performance, data arrival, incidents, maintenance cost, and changing business or regulatory requirements.

relations.reading: Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy affects Model Training Strategy because update triggers determine whether training is periodic, event-driven, or continuous
relations.rationale: The lifecycle policy determines how often and under what conditions training is initiated.

relations.reading: Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy affects Deployment Promotion Strategy because newly trained or replacement models require a controlled path into and out of production
relations.rationale: Retraining and rollback are only operationally safe when integrated with release and promotion mechanisms.

relations.reading: Model Retraining and Retirement Strategy requires Model Monitoring Strategy to be decided first
relations.rationale: Automated or evidence-based retraining and retirement depend on monitored drift, quality, incidents, and operational signals.

values.label: Scheduled retraining
values.description: Retraining at fixed calendar or data-volume intervals.

values.label: Trigger-based retraining
values.description: Retraining initiated by monitored drift, quality degradation, new labels, incidents, or business events.

values.label: Continuous updating
values.description: Frequent or ongoing model updates as new observations become available.

values.label: Champion-challenger replacement
values.description: Keeping a current champion while evaluating and promoting challenger models against it.

values.label: Model retirement and fallback
values.description: Archiving or disabling a model and reverting to a prior model, rule-based system, or safe default when required.

values.label: Stale model persistence
values.description: Continuing to use a model despite known degradation, changed conditions, or an inability to justify its continued suitability.

values.label: Lifecycle maintenance burden
values.description: An outcome describing the engineering, evaluation, governance, and infrastructure cost of keeping models current and safe.
